title: Living Underground in Beijing
summary: Josh and Chuck discuss Dixia Chang (Dixia Cheng), the underground city built beneath Beijing in 1969-1979 under Chairman Mao amid Sino-Soviet tensions after the Ussuri River border clashes. They cover the Sino-Soviet split, Mao's call to dig deep tunnels and store food, the tunnel network's scale and features, its closure and partial reopening as a tourist site, and the roughly million people (the "rat tribe") who now live in underground rooms as cheap housing. The episode closes with a listener mail correction about hard and soft rock mining and the pronunciation of "Lois."

segments.title: Opening banter and Sino-Soviet background
segments.summary: Hosts introduce the China edition and discuss the history of Chinese-Soviet relations, from tense border relations through the communist era, and how Mao publicly derided Soviet leaders as revisionists.

segments.title: 1969 border clashes and nuclear fears
segments.summary: The spring 1969 attack on a patrol near the Ussuri River left 24 Soviets dead; Soviet retaliation followed, and Mao responded by urging the population to build underground shelters against a possible Soviet invasion or nuclear attack.

segments.title: Pronouncing Dixia Chang
segments.summary: The hosts discuss how to pronounce Dixia Chang and joke about office pronunciation lookups.

segments.title: Building the underground city
segments.summary: Mao's slogan 'dig deep tunnels, store food, prepare for war' launched construction from 1969 to 1979. Citizens, including children, dug by hand, and blogger Anthony Tao's relatives recalled working on it. The network is about 18 miles of tunnels, with ventilation designed against fallout and shelters with recreation facilities.

segments.title: Access points, closure, and tourism
segments.summary: The complex had about 90 entrances, some in parks, homes, and shops, some needing a black light to read a map. The hosts compare it to a speakeasy. Its closure followed Mao's death, with a tourist opening that later stopped; it was closed for renovation before the 2008 Olympics, and the hosts could not confirm its current status.

segments.title: Rat Tribe and underground living today
segments.summary: Since around 2000, illegal squatting and residents have moved underground, numbering about a million people. Migrant workers pay around 50 to 70 US dollars a month for a small room, with communal toilets and showers. Sim Chi Yen's photo collection and the class divide with above-ground residents are discussed, along with mold issues.

segments.title: Tiananmen tunnels, listener mail and sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts mention rumors of tunnels linking to government buildings that were seemingly confirmed during the Tiananmen Square protests, then read a listener correction about hard and soft rock mining and the pronunciation of Lois, and sign off with contact information.
